chapter_text:
CHAPTER 5 - TISSUES AND OTHER LEVELS OF ORGANIZATION

Introduction

A single cell is the basic unit of life, but a large multicellular plant or animal is far more than a bag of independent cells. As body size increases, cells become specialised and share out the work of the body. Cells of one kind group together to build tissues, tissues combine into organs, organs cooperate as organ systems, and the systems together make the whole organism. This chapter examines this HIERARCHY of biological organization and then studies, in detail, the main TISSUES of plants and of animals - what they are made of, where they are found, and what jobs they perform.

5.1 LEVELS OF BIOLOGICAL ORGANIZATION

Living matter is built up step by step in a definite sequence:
 - CELL: the smallest structural and functional unit of life (for example a nerve cell or a leaf mesophyll cell).
 - TISSUE: a group of similar (or closely related) cells that have a common origin and perform a common function (for example muscle tissue).
 - ORGAN: a structure made of two or more kinds of tissue working together for a particular function (for example the heart, the leaf).
 - ORGAN SYSTEM: several organs cooperating to carry out a major body function (for example the digestive system).
 - ORGANISM: the complete living individual formed by all the organ systems working together.

This progression - cell to tissue to organ to organ system to organism - shows the principle of DIVISION OF LABOUR: as we move up the levels, structures become more specialised, so the whole body works more efficiently. Single-celled organisms carry out every life process within one cell, but in complex organisms different tissues take over different tasks.

5.2 WHAT IS A TISSUE?

A TISSUE is a group of cells, usually of similar structure and common origin, that act together to perform a particular function. The study of tissues is called HISTOLOGY. In flowering plants tissues are broadly classed as MERISTEMATIC (dividing) or PERMANENT (non-dividing). In animals the four basic tissue types are EPITHELIAL, CONNECTIVE, MUSCULAR and NERVOUS.

5.3 PLANT TISSUES: MERISTEMATIC TISSUE

MERISTEMATIC tissue (a MERISTEM) consists of small, thin-walled, actively dividing cells that are packed closely together with no intercellular spaces. The cells are roughly isodiametric (equal-sided), have dense cytoplasm, large prominent nuclei, and small or no vacuoles; they lack stored food and their walls are of thin cellulose. Their job is GROWTH - they add new cells to the plant body. Meristems are classified by POSITION:
 - APICAL MERISTEM: found at the growing tips (apices) of roots and shoots. It brings about PRIMARY GROWTH, increasing the LENGTH of the plant.
 - INTERCALARY MERISTEM: located between mature (permanent) tissues, typically at the bases of leaves or internodes (as in grasses). It also adds to length and lets grass regrow after grazing or mowing.
 - LATERAL MERISTEM: found along the sides of stems and roots, arranged as cylinders. Examples are the vascular CAMBIUM and the cork cambium. Lateral meristems bring about SECONDARY GROWTH, increasing the GIRTH (thickness) of the plant.

5.4 PLANT TISSUES: PERMANENT TISSUE

When meristematic cells stop dividing, enlarge and take on a definite shape and function, they form PERMANENT tissue. Permanent tissues are either SIMPLE (made of one kind of cell) or COMPLEX (made of more than one kind of cell).

(a) SIMPLE PERMANENT TISSUES

PARENCHYMA is the most common and least specialised tissue. Its cells are living, thin-walled (cellulose), roughly oval or round, with small intercellular spaces. Parenchyma stores food and water, carries out photosynthesis when it contains chloroplasts (then called CHLORENCHYMA), and provides packing and support to soft organs. In aquatic plants a parenchyma with large air spaces, called AERENCHYMA, gives buoyancy.

COLLENCHYMA is a living tissue that gives FLEXIBLE mechanical support to young growing parts such as the stalks of leaves and young stems. Its cells are elongated and are thickened at the CORNERS with extra cellulose and pectin. Because collenchyma is living and can stretch, it supports organs while still allowing them to bend and grow.

SCLERENCHYMA provides HARD, rigid support and consists of DEAD cells with thick, uniformly LIGNIFIED walls and no living contents; the cell cavity (lumen) is often greatly reduced. There are two forms: FIBRES, which are long, narrow cells with pointed ends (they give strength and are the source of jute, hemp and flax), and SCLEREIDS (stone cells), which are short and irregular and make the gritty texture of pears and the hard shells of nuts and seed coats.

(b) COMPLEX PERMANENT TISSUES

Complex tissues contain more than one type of cell that work together as a unit; they are the conducting (vascular) tissues XYLEM and PHLOEM.

XYLEM conducts WATER and dissolved MINERALS upward from the roots to the rest of the plant and also gives mechanical strength. It is made of four kinds of elements:
 - TRACHEIDS: elongated dead cells with tapering ends and lignified walls; water passes from one to the next through pits.
 - VESSELS (tracheae): long tubes formed by many dead cells joined end to end, their cross walls dissolved to make a continuous pipe; they are the chief water-conducting channels of flowering plants.
 - XYLEM PARENCHYMA: living cells that store food and help in short-distance water movement.
 - XYLEM FIBRES: dead sclerenchyma cells that give extra support.
Because tracheids and vessels are dead and hollow, xylem transport is a one-way, upward flow.

PHLOEM conducts FOOD (mainly sugars made in the leaves) to all parts of the plant; this movement is called TRANSLOCATION and can go up or down. Phloem also has four elements:
 - SIEVE TUBES: long tubes of living cells joined end to end, whose end walls are perforated like a sieve (SIEVE PLATES); mature sieve tube cells lack a nucleus.
 - COMPANION CELLS: living cells with a nucleus lying beside each sieve tube; they control the activity of the enucleate sieve tube and load sugars into it.
 - PHLOEM PARENCHYMA: living cells that store food and other substances.
 - PHLOEM FIBRES: the only dead elements of phloem, giving mechanical support.

5.5 TISSUE SYSTEMS OF PLANTS

On a larger scale, the tissues of a plant are grouped into three TISSUE SYSTEMS:
 - EPIDERMAL (DERMAL) TISSUE SYSTEM: the outermost protective layer - the epidermis - usually one cell thick and covered by a waterproof CUTICLE. It bears STOMATA (guarded pores for gas exchange), root hairs and other outgrowths.
 - GROUND (FUNDAMENTAL) TISSUE SYSTEM: all the tissue between the epidermis and the vascular tissue - mostly parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. It includes the cortex, pith and mesophyll and carries out photosynthesis, storage and support.
 - VASCULAR (CONDUCTING) TISSUE SYSTEM: the xylem and phloem, arranged in vascular bundles, that transport water, minerals and food through the plant body.

5.6 ANIMAL TISSUES: EPITHELIAL TISSUE

EPITHELIAL tissue (epithelium) covers the outside of the body and lines its internal cavities, tubes and organs. Its cells are packed tightly with almost no intercellular material and rest on a non-cellular BASEMENT MEMBRANE. Epithelium protects underlying parts and takes part in absorption, secretion and exchange. It is classified by the shape and layering of its cells:

SIMPLE EPITHELIUM (a single layer of cells):
 - SQUAMOUS epithelium: flat, thin, plate-like cells fitted together like floor tiles; it forms delicate linings where diffusion occurs, such as the walls of air sacs (alveoli) of the lungs and the walls of blood capillaries.
 - CUBOIDAL epithelium: cube-shaped cells; found in kidney tubules and the ducts of glands, where it helps in absorption and secretion.
 - COLUMNAR epithelium: tall, pillar-like cells; lines the stomach and intestine, where it absorbs nutrients and secretes mucus and enzymes.
 - CILIATED epithelium: cuboidal or columnar cells whose free surface bears CILIA (fine hair-like processes). The beating cilia move mucus, fluids or particles in one direction; found in the wind-pipe (trachea) and the oviduct.

COMPOUND (STRATIFIED) EPITHELIUM has many layers of cells and mainly PROTECTS against wear and tear, chemicals and drying; the outer skin (epidermis) and the lining of the mouth and oesophagus are examples.

GLANDULAR EPITHELIUM is formed when columnar or cuboidal cells become specialised to SECRETE substances such as mucus, enzymes or hormones; the cells may form single gland cells (goblet cells) or multicellular glands.

5.7 CONNECTIVE TISSUE

CONNECTIVE tissue is the most abundant and widely spread animal tissue. It binds, supports, packs and connects other tissues and organs. Its hallmark is that cells lie scattered in an abundant non-living MATRIX (intercellular substance) that the cells themselves secrete; the matrix may be jelly-like, fibrous, firm or fluid. The main kinds are:

LOOSE CONNECTIVE TISSUE has a soft matrix with loosely arranged fibres and cells.
 - AREOLAR tissue fills spaces inside organs, supports and repairs, and joins skin to muscle; it contains fibroblast cells (which make fibres), mast cells and macrophages.
 - ADIPOSE tissue is packed with fat-storing cells; it lies below the skin and around organs, storing energy and acting as an insulator and cushion.

DENSE CONNECTIVE TISSUE has closely packed fibres and forms strong cords and sheets:
 - TENDONS join muscle to bone; LIGAMENTS join bone to bone.

SPECIALISED (SUPPORTIVE and FLUID) CONNECTIVE TISSUES:
 - CARTILAGE has a firm yet flexible matrix (chondrin) in which cells called CHONDROCYTES lie in small spaces (lacunae). It supports and gives shape - found at the tips of the nose, in the external ear (pinna), between the vertebrae and at the ends of long bones. It also forms the skeleton of the young embryo.
 - BONE is a hard, rigid tissue whose matrix is hardened by deposits of CALCIUM and PHOSPHATE salts. Bone cells (OSTEOCYTES) lie in lacunae arranged in concentric rings around central (Haversian) canals that carry blood vessels and nerves. Bone forms the skeleton, protects organs (skull, ribs) and stores minerals.
 - BLOOD is a FLUID connective tissue with a liquid matrix called PLASMA (about 55% of blood; water with proteins, salts, glucose, hormones and wastes). Suspended in plasma are the formed elements: RED BLOOD CELLS (erythrocytes/RBC), which contain the pigment HAEMOGLOBIN and carry oxygen; WHITE BLOOD CELLS (leucocytes/WBC), which defend the body against disease; and PLATELETS (thrombocytes), tiny fragments that help the blood to CLOT. Blood transports gases, nutrients, wastes and hormones and helps in defence and temperature control.

5.8 MUSCULAR TISSUE

MUSCULAR tissue is made of long, contractile cells called MUSCLE FIBRES, rich in the proteins that let them shorten and produce movement. There are three types:
 - SKELETAL (STRIATED / VOLUNTARY) muscle is attached to bones and moves the skeleton. Its fibres are long, cylindrical, UNBRANCHED and MULTINUCLEATE, and show alternating light and dark bands (STRIATIONS). It is under our conscious (voluntary) control and tires quickly.
 - SMOOTH (UNSTRIATED / INVOLUNTARY) muscle has spindle-shaped cells, each with a SINGLE central nucleus and NO striations. It is found in the walls of the stomach, intestine, blood vessels and urinary bladder, works involuntarily (not under our will), and moves food, blood and other materials slowly.
 - CARDIAC muscle forms the wall of the HEART. Its fibres are cylindrical, BRANCHED and joined end to end at INTERCALATED DISCS, are striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary like smooth muscle, and contract rhythmically and tirelessly throughout life.

5.9 NERVOUS TISSUE

NERVOUS tissue receives stimuli and conducts impulses rapidly from one part of the body to another, allowing quick control and coordination. Its basic unit is the NEURON (nerve cell), which has:
 - a CELL BODY (cyton) containing the nucleus and cytoplasm;
 - many short branched processes, the DENDRITES, that receive impulses and carry them TOWARD the cell body; and
 - a single long process, the AXON, that carries the impulse AWAY from the cell body to the next cell.
The junction where the axon of one neuron meets the next cell is a SYNAPSE. Supporting cells called NEUROGLIA (glial cells) hold the neurons in place, nourish and protect them, and do not conduct impulses themselves. Nervous tissue makes up the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves.

5.10 ORGANS AND ORGAN SYSTEMS

Different tissues combine to build ORGANS. For example, the STOMACH is an organ built from epithelial tissue (its lining and glands), muscular tissue (to churn food), connective tissue (to bind and support) and nervous tissue (to control its activity). A LEAF is a plant organ built of epidermal, ground (mesophyll) and vascular tissues. Organs that cooperate on a common task form an ORGAN SYSTEM - for instance the digestive system (mouth, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas) or the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels). All the organ systems together make the complete ORGANISM. This tissue-organ-system arrangement lets a complex body divide its labour and function as an integrated whole.

SUMMARY

- Living bodies are organised in a hierarchy: cell to tissue to organ to organ system to organism, showing division of labour.
- A tissue is a group of cells of common origin performing a common function; plant tissues are meristematic or permanent, animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.
- Meristematic tissue is made of small dividing cells; apical (tips, primary growth/length), intercalary (leaf/internode bases), and lateral (cambium, secondary growth/girth).
- Simple permanent plant tissues: parenchyma (living, storage/photosynthesis), collenchyma (living, thickened at corners, flexible support), sclerenchyma (dead, lignified, hard support - fibres and sclereids).
- Complex tissues: xylem (tracheids, vessels, parenchyma, fibres) carries water and minerals upward; phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres) translocates food.
- Plant tissue systems: epidermal (protection, with cuticle and stomata), ground (storage, photosynthesis, support), vascular (xylem and phloem).
- Epithelial tissue covers and lines; simple (squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated), compound (protective), and glandular (secretory), all resting on a basement membrane.
- Connective tissue has cells scattered in a matrix: areolar and adipose (loose), tendons and ligaments (dense), cartilage and bone (skeletal), and blood (plasma with RBC, WBC and platelets).
- Muscular tissue: skeletal (striated, voluntary, multinucleate), smooth (unstriated, involuntary), cardiac (branched, striated, involuntary, intercalated discs).
- Nervous tissue conducts impulses; a neuron has a cell body, dendrites (receive) and an axon (transmit), supported by neuroglia.
- Different tissues build organs (stomach, leaf), organs build organ systems, and organ systems build the whole organism.

topics.name: Levels of Organization and Meristematic Tissue
topics.description: The hierarchy of biological organization (cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism) and the principle of division of labour; the definition of a tissue; and meristematic tissue - apical, intercalary and lateral (cambium) meristems and their roles in primary and secondary growth.

topics.name: Simple Permanent Plant Tissues
topics.description: Simple permanent plant tissues made of a single cell type: parenchyma (living, storage and photosynthesis), collenchyma (living, corner-thickened, flexible support) and sclerenchyma (dead, lignified, rigid support - fibres and sclereids).

topics.name: Complex Permanent Tissues and Tissue Systems
topics.description: Complex permanent tissues xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, fibres) and phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, fibres), and the three plant tissue systems - epidermal, ground and vascular.

topics.name: Animal Epithelial Tissue
topics.description: Animal epithelial tissue: simple epithelium (squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated), compound (stratified) epithelium and glandular epithelium; their structure, locations and functions of protection, absorption and secretion.

topics.name: Connective Tissue (incl. Blood, Bone, Cartilage)
topics.description: Connective tissue with cells in a matrix: loose (areolar, adipose), dense (tendons, ligaments) and specialised connective tissues - cartilage, bone, and blood (plasma with red cells, white cells and platelets).

topics.name: Muscular and Nervous Tissue
topics.description: Muscular tissue (skeletal/striated, smooth/unstriated and cardiac) and nervous tissue (the neuron with cell body, dendrites and axon, and supporting neuroglia), including their structure and functions.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Levels of Organization and Meristematic Tissue
learning_outcomes.description: Describe the levels of biological organization from cell to organism and the meaning of division of labour, define a tissue, and describe meristematic tissue and its apical, intercalary and lateral types.
Distinguish the simple permanent plant tissues parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma by their structure, wall thickenings, living/dead nature and functions.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Complex Permanent Tissues and Tissue Systems
learning_outcomes.description: Describe the complex permanent tissues xylem and phloem, naming their component cells and explaining how each conducts water/minerals or food.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Complex Permanent Tissues and Tissue Systems
learning_outcomes.description: Compare xylem with phloem and relate the three plant tissue systems (epidermal, ground, vascular) to their protective, fundamental and conducting functions.
Classify epithelial tissue into simple (squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated), compound and glandular types and relate each to its location and function.
Describe connective tissues - areolar, adipose, tendons, ligaments, cartilage, bone and blood - in terms of cells, matrix and function.
Apply knowledge of connective tissue, especially blood (plasma, red cells, white cells, platelets), bone and cartilage, to explain their roles in transport, support and defence.
Distinguish the three types of muscular tissue and describe the structure of a neuron and the role of nervous tissue and neuroglia in coordination.

chapter_summary.title: Tissues and other Levels of Organization - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Biology (314) summary for the lesson on Tissues and other Levels of Organization. It develops the hierarchy of organization from cell to organism, defines a tissue, and surveys the plant tissues (meristematic and permanent - simple and complex - and the tissue systems) and the four animal tissues (epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous), ending with organs and organ systems.

branches.label: Levels of Organization
details: Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ system -> Organism
Tissue = group of similar cells, common origin and function

branches.label: Epithelial Tissue
details: Covers and lines; rests on basement membrane

branches.label: Connective Tissue
