Cartilage, bone, and blood (plasma, RBC, WBC, platelets)

sections.heading: Levels of organization and meristematic tissue
bullets: The body is organised as cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism, illustrating division of labour.
A tissue is a group of cells of common origin performing a common function; plant tissues are meristematic or permanent.

Meristematic tissue has small, thin-walled, dividing cells; apical meristems give length (primary growth), intercalary meristems lie at leaf/internode bases, lateral meristems (cambium) give girth (secondary growth).

sections.heading: Simple and complex permanent plant tissues
bullets: Parenchyma is living and thin-walled, doing storage and (as chlorenchyma) photosynthesis; collenchyma is living with corner thickenings for flexible support.
Sclerenchyma is dead with thick lignified walls for rigid support, as fibres and sclereids (stone cells).
Xylem (tracheids, vessels, parenchyma, fibres) carries water and minerals upward; phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres) translocates food.

sections.heading: Epithelial tissue
bullets: Epithelium covers the body and lines cavities, tightly packed on a basement membrane, doing protection, absorption and secretion.
Simple epithelium is one layer: squamous (alveoli, capillaries), cuboidal (kidney tubules), columnar (intestine), ciliated (trachea, oviduct).
Compound (stratified) epithelium protects (skin, mouth); glandular epithelium secretes mucus, enzymes and hormones.

sections.heading: Connective tissue
bullets: Connective tissue has few cells in an abundant matrix; areolar and adipose are loose, tendons and ligaments are dense.
Cartilage (chondrocytes in a firm matrix) and bone (osteocytes in a matrix hardened by calcium salts) support the body.
Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma with red cells (haemoglobin, carry oxygen), white cells (defence) and platelets (clotting).

sections.heading: Muscular and nervous tissue; organs
bullets: Skeletal muscle is striated, voluntary and multinucleate; smooth muscle is unstriated and involuntary; cardiac muscle is branched, striated, involuntary with intercalated discs.
A neuron has a cell body, dendrites (receive impulses) and an axon (transmit impulses); neuroglia support the neurons.
Different tissues build organs (stomach, leaf), organs build organ systems, and organ systems build the whole organism.

key_takeaways: The organization of life rises from cell to tissue to organ to organ system to organism, sharing out the body's work.
A tissue is a group of cells with a common origin and function; plants have meristematic and permanent tissues, animals have four basic tissues.
Meristems are apical (length), intercalary (leaf/internode bases) and lateral/cambium (girth); permanent tissue is simple (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) or complex (xylem, phloem).
Xylem conducts water and minerals upward; phloem translocates food; plant tissue systems are epidermal, ground and vascular.
Epithelium covers and lines (simple, compound, glandular) resting on a basement membrane, while connective tissue binds and supports with cells set in a matrix.
Blood is a fluid connective tissue of plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets; cartilage and bone are supportive connective tissues.
Muscular tissue (skeletal, smooth, cardiac) produces movement and nervous tissue (neurons and neuroglia) conducts impulses for coordination.

glossary.definition: A group of cells of similar structure and common origin that work together to perform a particular function.
Tissue of small, thin-walled, actively dividing cells responsible for growth; apical, intercalary or lateral in position.
Meristem at the tips of roots and shoots that causes primary growth, increasing the length of the plant.
Meristem along the sides of stems and roots (e.g. vascular cambium) that causes secondary growth, increasing girth.
A living, thin-walled simple tissue that stores food and water and, with chloroplasts, carries out photosynthesis.
A living simple tissue with cells thickened at the corners that gives flexible mechanical support to young organs.
A dead simple tissue with thick lignified walls that gives rigid support; occurs as fibres and sclereids.
A complex tissue (tracheids, vessels, parenchyma, fibres) that conducts water and minerals upward and gives support.
A complex tissue (sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres) that translocates food made in the leaves.
Tissue that covers the body and lines its cavities, resting on a basement membrane; protects, absorbs and secretes.
Tissue that binds and supports other tissues, with cells scattered in an abundant non-living matrix.
A supportive connective tissue with chondrocytes in a firm, flexible matrix; found in the nose, ear pinna and joints.
A fluid connective tissue of plasma carrying red cells (oxygen), white cells (defence) and platelets (clotting).
The structural and functional unit of nervous tissue, with a cell body, dendrites that receive and an axon that transmits impulses.
The junction joining branched cardiac muscle fibres end to end, allowing coordinated rhythmic contraction of the heart.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Tissues and other Levels of Organization (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. For diagrams described in words, name the structures clearly. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Arrange the levels of biological organization in the correct order from the smallest to the largest and define a tissue.
questions.answer: The levels, from smallest to largest, are: cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism. A tissue is a group of cells, usually of similar structure and common origin, that work together to perform a particular function (for example muscle tissue). This arrangement shows division of labour, because different tissues take over different tasks in a complex body.
questions.explanation: Correct sequence plus the definition of a tissue.

questions.question: Name the three types of meristematic tissue by their position and state what each does.
questions.answer: Apical meristem lies at the tips of roots and shoots and causes primary growth (increase in length). Intercalary meristem lies between mature tissues, at the bases of leaves or internodes (as in grasses), and also adds to length. Lateral meristem lies along the sides of stems and roots (for example the vascular cambium) and causes secondary growth (increase in girth or thickness).
questions.explanation: Apical, intercalary and lateral with position and function.

questions.question: Distinguish between collenchyma and sclerenchyma with respect to living nature, wall thickening and function.
questions.answer: Collenchyma is a LIVING tissue whose cells are thickened at the CORNERS with cellulose and pectin; it gives flexible mechanical support to young growing organs while still allowing them to bend. Sclerenchyma is made of DEAD cells with thick, uniformly LIGNIFIED walls and no living contents; it gives hard, rigid support and strength (as fibres and sclereids).
questions.explanation: Living vs dead, corner vs uniform lignified thickening, flexible vs rigid support.

questions.question: Name the four kinds of cells found in xylem and state the main function of xylem.
questions.answer: Xylem contains tracheids, vessels (tracheae), xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres. Its main function is to conduct water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the rest of the plant, and to give mechanical strength. Tracheids and vessels are dead and hollow and form the conducting channels, parenchyma stores food, and fibres provide support.
questions.explanation: Four elements plus the conduction of water/minerals.

questions.question: Compare xylem and phloem under the headings: cells present, material conducted, direction of flow, and living or dead conducting cells.
questions.answer: CELLS PRESENT: Xylem has tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and fibres; phloem has sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and fibres. MATERIAL CONDUCTED: Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals; phloem conducts food (mainly sugars), a process called translocation. DIRECTION OF FLOW: Xylem flow is essentially one-way, upward from roots to shoot; phloem flow can be both upward and downward to wherever food is needed. LIVING OR DEAD CONDUCTING CELLS: The conducting cells of xylem (tracheids and vessels) are DEAD and hollow; the conducting cells of phloem (sieve tubes) are LIVING, though a mature sieve tube lacks a nucleus and is controlled by its companion cell.
questions.explanation: Four-way comparison covering cells, material, direction and living/dead nature.

questions.question: Where in the body is (a) squamous epithelium and (b) ciliated epithelium found, and what does each do?
questions.answer: (a) Squamous epithelium is made of thin, flat cells and lines delicate surfaces where materials diffuse, such as the walls of the alveoli (air sacs) of the lungs and the walls of blood capillaries; it allows easy exchange of gases and materials. (b) Ciliated epithelium has cilia on its free surface and lines the wind-pipe (trachea) and the oviduct; the beating cilia move mucus, particles or fluids in one direction.
questions.explanation: Locations and functions of squamous and ciliated epithelium.

questions.question: State one function each of red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
questions.answer: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen (and some carbon dioxide) around the body. White blood cells (leucocytes) defend the body against disease-causing germs. Platelets (thrombocytes) help the blood to clot when a blood vessel is injured, stopping bleeding.
questions.explanation: One correct function for each formed element of blood.

questions.question: Why is blood considered a connective tissue? Name its liquid matrix.
questions.answer: Blood is considered a connective tissue because it has cells (red cells, white cells) and cell fragments (platelets) suspended in an abundant non-living intercellular matrix, and it connects and transports materials between different parts of the body - the defining features of connective tissue. Its liquid matrix is called PLASMA.
questions.explanation: Cells in a matrix + connecting/transport role; matrix is plasma.

questions.question: Describe the three types of muscular tissue, mentioning for each its striations, control (voluntary/involuntary) and one location.
questions.answer: SKELETAL (striated / voluntary) muscle has long, cylindrical, unbranched, multinucleate fibres with clear striations (light and dark bands); it is under conscious (voluntary) control and is attached to bones (for example the biceps of the arm). SMOOTH (unstriated / involuntary) muscle has spindle-shaped cells each with a single nucleus and no striations; it works involuntarily and is found in the walls of the stomach, intestine and blood vessels. CARDIAC muscle has cylindrical, branched fibres joined at intercalated discs; it is striated but involuntary and forms the wall of the heart, contracting rhythmically throughout life.
questions.explanation: Three types with striations, control and a location each.

questions.question: Draw (in words) and label the parts of a neuron, stating the direction in which impulses travel.
questions.answer: A neuron has a CELL BODY (cyton) that contains the nucleus and cytoplasm; from it arise many short, branched DENDRITES that RECEIVE impulses and carry them TOWARD the cell body; and one long AXON that carries the impulse AWAY from the cell body to the next cell. So the impulse travels: dendrite -> cell body -> axon -> synapse -> next neuron. Supporting neuroglia cells hold and nourish the neuron.
questions.explanation: Cell body, dendrites, axon and correct direction of impulse.

questions.question: The correct sequence of levels of organization from smallest to largest is:
options: Cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism
questions.answer: Cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism
questions.explanation: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, which form the organism.

questions.question: The smallest structural and functional unit of life is the:
questions.explanation: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living things.

questions.question: A group of similar cells of common origin performing a common function is a(n):
questions.explanation: A tissue is a group of similar cells with a common origin and function.

questions.question: The branch of biology that deals with the study of tissues is called:
questions.explanation: Histology is the study of tissues.

questions.question: Meristematic tissue is chiefly concerned with:
questions.explanation: Meristematic cells divide actively to add new cells, bringing about growth.

questions.question: Which feature is typical of meristematic cells?
options: Dense cytoplasm, large nuclei and thin walls
questions.answer: Dense cytoplasm, large nuclei and thin walls
questions.explanation: Dividing meristem cells are thin-walled with dense cytoplasm and prominent nuclei and little vacuolation.

questions.question: Increase in the LENGTH of a plant is brought about mainly by the:
questions.explanation: Apical meristems at root and shoot tips cause primary growth, increasing length.

questions.question: Increase in the GIRTH (thickness) of a stem is due to the:
questions.explanation: Lateral meristems such as the vascular cambium cause secondary growth (girth).

questions.question: Intercalary meristem is typically located:
options: At the bases of leaves or internodes
In the wood of old trees
questions.answer: At the bases of leaves or internodes
questions.explanation: Intercalary meristem lies between permanent tissues, at leaf/internode bases (as in grasses).

questions.question: The ability of grass to regrow quickly after being mown is due to its:
questions.explanation: Intercalary meristem at the leaf bases lets grass regrow after grazing or mowing.

questions.question: The vascular cambium is an example of a:
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium is a lateral meristem responsible for secondary growth.

questions.question: Progressive specialisation of cells for different jobs as we move up the levels of organization is called:
questions.explanation: Specialisation of tissues for different functions is called division of labour.

questions.question: The most common and least specialised simple plant tissue is:
questions.explanation: Parenchyma is the commonest, least specialised simple tissue.

questions.question: Parenchyma containing chloroplasts and carrying out photosynthesis is called:
questions.explanation: Photosynthetic parenchyma with chloroplasts is chlorenchyma.

questions.question: Parenchyma with large air spaces that gives buoyancy to aquatic plants is:
questions.explanation: Aerenchyma has large air spaces that make aquatic plants buoyant.

questions.question: Collenchyma cells are characteristically thickened at their:
questions.explanation: Collenchyma has extra cellulose/pectin deposited at the corners of the cells.

questions.question: Which tissue gives FLEXIBLE mechanical support to young growing stems and leaf stalks?
questions.explanation: Living collenchyma supports young organs yet lets them bend and grow.

questions.question: Sclerenchyma cells at maturity are:
questions.explanation: Mature sclerenchyma cells are dead with thick, lignified walls.

questions.question: The chemical substance that makes sclerenchyma walls hard and rigid is:
questions.explanation: Lignin thickens and hardens sclerenchyma cell walls.

questions.question: Jute, hemp and flax used to make ropes and fabric are commercial sources of sclerenchyma:
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma fibres are the source of jute, hemp and flax.

questions.question: The gritty texture of a pear fruit is due to short, hard cells called:
questions.explanation: Sclereids (stone cells) give pears their gritty texture.

questions.question: Which of these tissues is made of DEAD cells?
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma alone among these consists of dead cells.

questions.question: Storage of food and water in soft plant parts is mainly a function of:
questions.explanation: Thin-walled living parenchyma stores food and water.

questions.question: A simple permanent tissue is one that is made of:
options: More than one type of cell
questions.explanation: Simple tissues (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) contain a single cell type.

questions.question: Xylem conducts:
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and minerals upward from roots.

questions.question: The main food-conducting tissue in a plant is:
questions.explanation: Phloem translocates food (sugars) made in the leaves.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a component of xylem?
questions.explanation: Sieve tubes belong to phloem, not xylem.

questions.question: The chief water-conducting elements of flowering plants, formed of dead cells joined end to end with dissolved cross walls, are:
questions.explanation: Vessels (tracheae) are long tubes of dead cells with dissolved cross walls.

questions.question: The movement of food through phloem is called:
questions.explanation: The movement of food in phloem is termed translocation.

questions.question: A mature sieve tube cell is unusual because it lacks a:
questions.explanation: A mature sieve tube is living but has lost its nucleus.

questions.question: The cell that controls the activity of a sieve tube and loads sugar into it is the:
questions.explanation: The companion cell, with its nucleus, controls the enucleate sieve tube.

questions.question: The perforated end walls of sieve tubes are called:
questions.explanation: Sieve tubes join through perforated sieve plates.

questions.question: The ONLY dead element of phloem is the:
questions.explanation: Phloem fibres are the only dead cells of phloem; the rest are living.

questions.question: The outermost protective tissue system of a plant, covered by a cuticle, is the:
questions.explanation: The epidermal (dermal) tissue system protects and bears the cuticle and stomata.

questions.question: Stomata, the guarded pores for gas exchange, are part of the:
questions.explanation: Stomata occur in the epidermis, part of the epidermal tissue system.

questions.question: The cortex, pith and mesophyll of a plant belong to the:
questions.explanation: Ground (fundamental) tissue system includes cortex, pith and mesophyll.

questions.question: Xylem and phloem together make up the:
questions.explanation: The vascular tissue system is made of xylem and phloem.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts xylem and phloem?
options: Xylem conducts water upward; phloem conducts food up or down
Phloem conducts water; xylem conducts food
Both are made only of dead cells
questions.answer: Xylem conducts water upward; phloem conducts food up or down
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water/minerals upward (dead cells); phloem translocates food both ways (living cells).

questions.question: Epithelial tissue always rests on a non-cellular layer called the:
questions.explanation: Epithelium sits on a basement membrane.

questions.question: The thin, flat, tile-like cells that line the alveoli and blood capillaries form:
questions.explanation: Flat squamous epithelium lines alveoli and capillaries for easy diffusion.

questions.question: Cube-shaped epithelial cells lining the kidney tubules and gland ducts form:
questions.explanation: Cuboidal epithelium lines kidney tubules and gland ducts.

questions.question: The tall, pillar-like epithelium that lines the stomach and intestine is:
questions.explanation: Columnar epithelium lines the stomach and intestine for absorption and secretion.

questions.question: Cilia that sweep mucus along the wind-pipe are found on:
questions.explanation: Ciliated epithelium of the trachea moves mucus with its beating cilia.

questions.question: Which epithelium is best suited to surfaces where rapid diffusion of gases must occur?
questions.explanation: Thin squamous cells allow fast diffusion, as in the alveoli.

questions.question: Many-layered epithelium whose chief function is protection against wear and tear is:
questions.explanation: Compound (stratified) epithelium, as in skin, protects against wear.

questions.question: Epithelial cells specialised to secrete mucus, enzymes or hormones form:
questions.explanation: Glandular epithelium is specialised for secretion.

questions.question: The outer protective epidermis of the skin is an example of:
questions.explanation: Skin epidermis is a many-layered compound (stratified) epithelium.

questions.question: A single mucus-secreting gland cell scattered among columnar cells is a:
questions.explanation: Goblet cells are unicellular mucus-secreting glandular cells.

questions.question: A general function of epithelial tissue is to:
options: Cover and protect surfaces and take part in absorption and secretion
questions.answer: Cover and protect surfaces and take part in absorption and secretion
questions.explanation: Epithelium covers/lines and does protection, absorption and secretion.

questions.question: Ciliated epithelium in the oviduct helps to:
options: Move the egg along the tube
questions.answer: Move the egg along the tube
questions.explanation: Cilia of the oviduct epithelium move the egg toward the uterus.

questions.question: The defining feature of connective tissue is that its cells lie in an abundant:
questions.explanation: Connective tissue cells are scattered in a non-living intercellular matrix.

questions.question: The connective tissue that joins skin to muscle and fills spaces inside organs is:
questions.explanation: Areolar (loose) tissue fills spaces and joins skin to underlying muscle.

questions.question: Fat-storing connective tissue found below the skin is:
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue stores fat and insulates the body.

questions.question: A tendon connects:
questions.explanation: Tendons (dense connective tissue) join muscle to bone.

questions.question: A ligament connects:
questions.explanation: Ligaments join bone to bone at joints.

questions.question: The cells embedded in the firm matrix of cartilage are called:
questions.explanation: Cartilage cells are chondrocytes, lying in lacunae.

questions.question: Cartilage is found in all of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.explanation: The heart wall is cardiac muscle; cartilage is in nose, pinna and joints.

questions.question: The hardness of bone matrix is due to deposits of:
questions.explanation: Bone matrix is hardened by calcium and phosphate salts.

questions.question: Bone cells lying in lacunae around a central canal are called:
questions.explanation: Osteocytes are bone cells arranged around Haversian canals.

questions.question: Blood is classed as a connective tissue because it has cells suspended in a fluid matrix called:
questions.explanation: Blood's liquid matrix is plasma, making it a fluid connective tissue.

questions.question: The oxygen-carrying pigment present in red blood cells is:
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in RBCs carries oxygen.

questions.question: Blood cells that defend the body against disease are the:
questions.explanation: White blood cells (leucocytes) fight infection.

questions.question: The blood component that helps in clotting is the:
questions.explanation: Platelets (thrombocytes) help blood to clot.

questions.question: Roughly what fraction of the blood is plasma?
questions.explanation: Plasma makes up about 55% of the blood volume.

questions.question: Muscle that is attached to bones, striated and under our conscious control is:
questions.explanation: Skeletal (striated, voluntary) muscle moves the bones.

questions.question: Skeletal muscle fibres are:
questions.explanation: Skeletal fibres are long, cylindrical, unbranched and multinucleate.

questions.question: Spindle-shaped, unstriated muscle with a single nucleus found in the gut wall is:
questions.explanation: Smooth (unstriated, involuntary) muscle occurs in the gut wall.

questions.question: Muscle that is striated but involuntary and forms the wall of the heart is:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary, forming the heart wall.

questions.question: Intercalated discs are a special feature of:
questions.explanation: Branched cardiac fibres join at intercalated discs.

questions.question: The structural and functional unit of nervous tissue is the:
questions.explanation: The neuron (nerve cell) is the unit of nervous tissue.

questions.question: The short, branched processes of a neuron that RECEIVE impulses are the:
questions.explanation: Dendrites receive impulses and carry them toward the cell body.

questions.question: The single long process that carries an impulse AWAY from the cell body is the:
questions.explanation: The axon transmits the impulse away from the cell body.

questions.question: The junction between the axon of one neuron and the next cell is a:
questions.explanation: The synapse is the junction between neurons.

questions.question: Supporting cells of nervous tissue that nourish and protect neurons but do not conduct impulses are:
questions.explanation: Neuroglia (glial cells) support and protect neurons.

questions.question: Which muscle type does NOT tire and works continuously throughout life?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle contracts rhythmically and tirelessly throughout life.

questions.question: Meristematic cells have large vacuoles and are unable to divide.
questions.explanation: Meristematic cells have small or no vacuoles and divide actively.

questions.question: Apical meristem is responsible for increasing the length of the plant.
questions.explanation: Apical meristems at tips cause primary growth (length).

questions.question: Sclerenchyma is a living tissue thickened at the corners of its cells.
questions.explanation: That describes collenchyma; sclerenchyma is dead with uniformly lignified walls.

questions.question: Parenchyma with chloroplasts (chlorenchyma) can carry out photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Chlorenchyma contains chloroplasts and photosynthesises.

questions.question: The conducting cells of xylem (tracheids and vessels) are dead at maturity.
questions.explanation: Tracheids and vessels are dead, hollow, lignified cells.

questions.question: Companion cells are found in the xylem.
questions.explanation: Companion cells are part of the phloem, alongside sieve tubes.

questions.question: Squamous epithelium is thick and many-layered.
questions.explanation: Squamous epithelium is a single layer of thin, flat cells.

questions.question: A tendon joins one bone to another bone.
questions.explanation: A tendon joins muscle to bone; a ligament joins bone to bone.

questions.question: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen.
questions.explanation: RBCs carry oxygen using the pigment haemoglobin.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle is striated but works involuntarily.
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary.

questions.question: The sequence of organization is cell -> tissue -> organ -> ______ -> organism.
questions.explanation: Organs group into organ systems, which form the organism.

questions.question: ________ meristem lies between mature tissues, often at the bases of leaves and internodes.
questions.explanation: Intercalary meristem occurs between permanent tissues at leaf/internode bases.

questions.question: The lateral meristem responsible for secondary growth is the vascular ________.
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium is the lateral meristem for girth increase.

questions.question: ________ is the commonest simple tissue, being living and thin-walled and storing food.
questions.explanation: Parenchyma is the common living, thin-walled storage tissue.

questions.question: Sclerenchyma walls are hardened by the deposition of ________.
questions.explanation: Lignin thickens and hardens sclerenchyma walls.

questions.question: Short, hard sclerenchyma cells that give pears their gritty texture are called ________.
questions.explanation: Sclereids (stone cells) cause the gritty texture of pears.

questions.question: ________ conducts water and minerals upward, while phloem conducts food.
questions.explanation: Xylem transports water and minerals; phloem transports food.

questions.question: A mature sieve tube is controlled by its neighbouring ________ cell.
questions.explanation: Companion cells control the enucleate sieve tubes.

questions.question: Epithelial tissue rests on a non-cellular layer called the ________ membrane.
questions.explanation: Epithelium sits on a basement membrane.

questions.question: ________ epithelium bears cilia and lines the wind-pipe (trachea).
questions.explanation: Ciliated epithelium lines the trachea and moves mucus.

questions.question: The cells found in the firm matrix of cartilage are called ________.
questions.explanation: Chondrocytes are the cells of cartilage.

questions.question: The liquid matrix of blood is called ________.
questions.explanation: Plasma is the fluid matrix of blood.

questions.question: Tiny cell fragments that help blood to clot are the ________.
questions.explanation: Platelets (thrombocytes) help blood to clot.

questions.question: Branched cardiac muscle fibres are joined end to end at ________ discs.
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs connect cardiac muscle fibres.

questions.question: In a neuron, the ________ carries the impulse away from the cell body.
questions.explanation: The axon transmits the impulse away from the cell body.

questions.question: Define a tissue and give one example each of a plant tissue and an animal tissue.
questions.answer: A tissue is a group of cells, usually of similar structure and common origin, that work together to perform a particular function. An example of a plant tissue is parenchyma (or xylem); an example of an animal tissue is muscle tissue (or epithelial tissue).
questions.explanation: Definition plus one plant and one animal example.

questions.question: List four characteristics of meristematic cells.
questions.answer: Meristematic cells are (1) small and roughly isodiametric, (2) thin-walled (of cellulose) and closely packed with no intercellular spaces, (3) rich in dense cytoplasm with large prominent nuclei, and (4) have small or no vacuoles and divide actively to bring about growth.
questions.explanation: Any four correct features of meristematic cells.

questions.question: Differentiate between primary growth and secondary growth in plants.
questions.answer: Primary growth is the increase in LENGTH of the plant brought about by the APICAL meristems at the tips of roots and shoots. Secondary growth is the increase in GIRTH or thickness of stems and roots brought about by the LATERAL meristems (such as the vascular cambium). Primary growth lengthens the plant; secondary growth thickens it.
questions.explanation: Length vs girth; apical vs lateral meristem.

questions.question: Why is parenchyma considered a versatile tissue? Give three of its functions.
questions.answer: Parenchyma is versatile because its simple, living, thin-walled cells can take on several roles. Three functions are: (1) storage of food and water, (2) photosynthesis when it contains chloroplasts (chlorenchyma), and (3) providing packing and support to soft organs; aerenchyma also gives buoyancy to aquatic plants.
questions.explanation: Storage, photosynthesis, packing/support (or buoyancy).

questions.question: How is collenchyma suited to supporting young, growing organs?
questions.answer: Collenchyma is a LIVING tissue with cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin. Because it is living and its thickenings are uneven, it is strong yet FLEXIBLE and can stretch. This lets it support young stems and leaf stalks mechanically while still allowing them to bend and continue growing.
questions.explanation: Living, corner-thickened, flexible support permitting growth.

questions.question: Distinguish between fibres and sclereids, both of which are sclerenchyma.
questions.answer: Fibres are long, narrow sclerenchyma cells with pointed ends; they occur in strands and give strength (source of jute, hemp and flax). Sclereids (stone cells) are short, irregular, thick-walled cells; they make the gritty texture of pears and the hard shells of nuts and seed coats. Both are dead cells with lignified walls but differ in shape and length.
questions.explanation: Long pointed fibres vs short irregular sclereids.

questions.question: Name the four elements of phloem and give the function of each.
questions.answer: Phloem contains: (1) sieve tubes - living tubes joined by sieve plates that conduct food; (2) companion cells - nucleated cells beside sieve tubes that control them and load sugar; (3) phloem parenchyma - living cells that store food; and (4) phloem fibres - dead cells that give mechanical support.
questions.explanation: Four elements with correct functions.

questions.question: Explain why the conducting cells of xylem being dead does not prevent water transport.
questions.answer: The conducting cells of xylem - tracheids and vessels - are dead and empty at maturity, with lignified walls and their cross walls perforated or dissolved. Being hollow, they form continuous, unobstructed pipes through which water can move upward freely. Water transport is a physical pull (through the plant) and does not need living cytoplasm, so dead hollow cells are actually ideal for it.
questions.explanation: Dead hollow lignified tubes form open pipes; transport is physical.

questions.question: Name and briefly describe the three tissue systems of a plant.
questions.answer: (1) Epidermal (dermal) tissue system: the outer protective epidermis with a cuticle and stomata. (2) Ground (fundamental) tissue system: the tissue between epidermis and vascular tissue (cortex, pith, mesophyll) that does storage, photosynthesis and support. (3) Vascular (conducting) tissue system: the xylem and phloem that transport water, minerals and food.
questions.explanation: Epidermal (protection), ground (storage/support), vascular (conduction).

questions.question: Give three differences between xylem and phloem.
questions.answer: (1) Function: xylem conducts water and minerals, phloem conducts food. (2) Direction: xylem flow is upward only, phloem flow can be both up and down. (3) Nature of conducting cells: xylem's conducting cells (tracheids, vessels) are dead, whereas phloem's conducting cells (sieve tubes) are living. (Xylem also gives more mechanical support.)
questions.explanation: Function, direction and living/dead conducting cells.

questions.question: What is epithelial tissue? State its two general functions.
questions.answer: Epithelial tissue is a tightly packed tissue that covers the outer surface of the body and lines its internal cavities, tubes and organs, resting on a basement membrane. Two of its general functions are: (1) protection of the underlying parts, and (2) absorption and secretion (and exchange) of materials.
questions.explanation: Definition + protection and absorption/secretion.

questions.question: Match each simple epithelium to a location: squamous, cuboidal, columnar.
questions.answer: Squamous epithelium - the walls of the alveoli of the lungs and of blood capillaries (for diffusion). Cuboidal epithelium - the kidney tubules and the ducts of glands (for absorption and secretion). Columnar epithelium - the lining of the stomach and intestine (for absorption and secretion).
questions.explanation: Squamous-alveoli/capillaries, cuboidal-kidney tubules, columnar-intestine.

questions.question: How does compound (stratified) epithelium differ from simple epithelium, and where is it found?
questions.answer: Simple epithelium is a SINGLE layer of cells and is chiefly concerned with diffusion, absorption and secretion. Compound (stratified) epithelium has MANY layers of cells and its main job is PROTECTION against wear and tear, chemicals and drying. It is found in the outer skin (epidermis) and the lining of the mouth and oesophagus.
questions.explanation: Single vs many layers; absorption/secretion vs protection; skin/mouth.

questions.question: What is a matrix, and why is the presence of a matrix important in connective tissue?
questions.answer: The matrix is the abundant non-living intercellular substance in which the cells of a connective tissue lie scattered; it is secreted by the cells themselves and may be jelly-like, fibrous, firm or fluid. It is important because the nature of the matrix decides the properties and function of the tissue - a firm matrix makes cartilage supportive, a salt-hardened matrix makes bone rigid, and a fluid matrix (plasma) lets blood transport materials.
questions.explanation: Matrix = intercellular substance; its nature sets the tissue's function.

questions.question: Describe adipose tissue and state two of its functions.
questions.answer: Adipose tissue is a loose connective tissue packed with fat-storing cells, found below the skin and around internal organs. Two of its functions are: (1) it STORES energy in the form of fat, and (2) it acts as an INSULATOR against heat loss and as a CUSHION protecting the organs it surrounds.
questions.explanation: Fat-storing loose tissue; energy store + insulation/cushioning.

questions.question: Compare cartilage and bone under two headings: nature of the matrix and the cells present.
questions.answer: NATURE OF MATRIX: Cartilage has a firm but FLEXIBLE matrix (chondrin); bone has a HARD, rigid matrix hardened by deposits of calcium and phosphate salts. CELLS PRESENT: Cartilage cells are CHONDROCYTES lying in lacunae; bone cells are OSTEOCYTES lying in lacunae arranged around central (Haversian) canals. Both are supportive connective tissues, but bone is much harder than cartilage.
questions.explanation: Flexible chondrin/chondrocytes vs hard salt matrix/osteocytes.

questions.question: List the components of blood and give one function of the plasma.
questions.answer: Blood consists of a fluid matrix called PLASMA in which are suspended the formed elements: red blood cells (RBC), white blood cells (WBC) and platelets. One function of plasma is to TRANSPORT dissolved substances - nutrients such as glucose, wastes, hormones, proteins and salts - around the body (it also helps distribute heat).
questions.explanation: Plasma + RBC, WBC, platelets; plasma transports dissolved substances.

questions.question: A person with a low platelet count bruises easily and bleeds for a long time after a cut. Explain why.
questions.answer: Platelets (thrombocytes) are the blood cell fragments responsible for CLOTTING. When a blood vessel is injured, platelets gather at the wound and help form a clot that seals it and stops the bleeding. If the platelet count is low, clots form slowly or poorly, so even small injuries keep bleeding and blood leaking under the skin causes easy bruising.
questions.explanation: Low platelets = poor clotting = prolonged bleeding and bruising.

questions.question: Give three differences between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle.
questions.answer: (1) Striations: skeletal muscle is striated (banded), smooth muscle is unstriated. (2) Control: skeletal muscle is voluntary (under conscious control), smooth muscle is involuntary. (3) Shape/nuclei: skeletal fibres are long, cylindrical and multinucleate, whereas smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single nucleus. (Location: skeletal muscle is attached to bones; smooth muscle is in the gut and blood-vessel walls.)
questions.explanation: Striations, voluntary/involuntary, shape/nuclei.

questions.question: Draw (in words) a neuron and label its three main parts, giving the function of each.
questions.answer: A neuron has: (1) a CELL BODY (cyton) - contains the nucleus and cytoplasm and controls the cell; (2) DENDRITES - short, branched processes arising from the cell body that RECEIVE impulses and carry them toward the cell body; and (3) an AXON - a single long process that carries the impulse AWAY from the cell body to the next cell across a synapse.
questions.explanation: Cell body (control), dendrites (receive), axon (transmit).

questions.question: What are neuroglia and how do they differ from neurons?
questions.answer: Neuroglia (glial cells) are the supporting cells of nervous tissue. They hold the neurons in place, and nourish, insulate and protect them. Unlike neurons, neuroglia do NOT conduct nerve impulses themselves; their role is purely supportive, whereas neurons are the impulse-conducting units of the tissue.
questions.explanation: Supporting cells; do not conduct impulses, unlike neurons.

questions.question: Why is cardiac muscle described as sharing features of both skeletal and smooth muscle?
questions.answer: Cardiac muscle is STRIATED, like skeletal muscle, showing light and dark bands. But it is INVOLUNTARY, like smooth muscle, working automatically without conscious control. In addition its fibres are branched and joined at intercalated discs and contract rhythmically and tirelessly throughout life. So it combines the striations of skeletal muscle with the involuntary action of smooth muscle.
questions.explanation: Striated like skeletal, involuntary like smooth.

questions.question: Explain the levels of biological organization from the cell to the organism, and state how they illustrate the principle of division of labour.
questions.answer: Living matter is built up in a definite sequence of levels. The CELL is the smallest structural and functional unit of life (e.g. a nerve cell). A TISSUE is a group of similar cells of common origin performing a common function (e.g. muscle tissue). An ORGAN is made of two or more kinds of tissue working together for a particular function (e.g. the heart, the leaf). An ORGAN SYSTEM is several organs cooperating for a major body function (e.g. the digestive system). The ORGANISM is the complete individual formed by all the organ systems together. As we move up these levels, structures become progressively more SPECIALISED, so different parts take over different tasks - this is the principle of DIVISION OF LABOUR. In a single-celled organism one cell does everything, but in a complex body the work is shared out: epithelium covers and secretes, muscle contracts, nerves coordinate, and so on. This specialisation makes the whole body work far more efficiently.
questions.explanation: Five levels defined + division of labour explained.

questions.question: Describe the three types of simple permanent plant tissue, contrasting their living nature, wall thickenings and functions.
questions.answer: The three simple permanent tissues are parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. PARENCHYMA is a LIVING tissue of thin-walled (cellulose) cells with small intercellular spaces; it stores food and water, carries out photosynthesis when it has chloroplasts (chlorenchyma), and provides packing to soft organs. COLLENCHYMA is also LIVING; its cells are thickened at the CORNERS with extra cellulose and pectin, so it gives flexible mechanical support to young stems and leaf stalks while still allowing them to bend and grow. SCLERENCHYMA is made of DEAD cells with thick, uniformly LIGNIFIED walls and no living contents; it gives hard, rigid support and occurs as long fibres (giving jute, hemp, flax) and short sclereids (stone cells of pears and nut shells). Thus the three grade from soft living storage tissue (parenchyma), through flexible living support (collenchyma), to hard dead support (sclerenchyma).
questions.explanation: Three tissues contrasted on living nature, thickening and function.

questions.question: Describe the structure and function of xylem and phloem, naming their component cells.
questions.answer: XYLEM conducts water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots and also gives mechanical strength. It has four elements: TRACHEIDS (elongated dead cells with tapering ends and pitted lignified walls), VESSELS (long tubes of dead cells joined end to end with dissolved cross walls - the chief water channels of flowering plants), XYLEM PARENCHYMA (living cells that store food and help short-distance water movement) and XYLEM FIBRES (dead cells that give support). PHLOEM conducts food (sugars) made in the leaves to all parts of the plant, a process called translocation that can go up or down. It also has four elements: SIEVE TUBES (living tubes joined by perforated sieve plates; mature ones lack a nucleus), COMPANION CELLS (nucleated cells beside each sieve tube that control it and load sugar), PHLOEM PARENCHYMA (living storage cells) and PHLOEM FIBRES (the only dead cells of phloem, giving support). Together, xylem and phloem form the vascular tissue that supplies the whole plant with water and food.
questions.explanation: Both tissues: elements + functions.

questions.question: Classify epithelial tissue and describe each type with a location and a function.
questions.answer: Epithelial tissue covers and lines body surfaces and rests on a basement membrane. It is classified as follows. SIMPLE (single-layered): (a) SQUAMOUS - flat tile-like cells lining alveoli and capillaries, allowing diffusion; (b) CUBOIDAL - cube-shaped cells in kidney tubules and gland ducts, for absorption and secretion; (c) COLUMNAR - tall cells lining the stomach and intestine, for absorption and secretion of mucus and enzymes; (d) CILIATED - cells bearing cilia in the trachea and oviduct, moving mucus or the egg in one direction. COMPOUND (STRATIFIED): many-layered epithelium, as in the skin epidermis and the lining of the mouth, whose main job is protection against wear and tear. GLANDULAR: columnar or cuboidal cells specialised to secrete mucus, enzymes or hormones (e.g. goblet cells and glands). Thus epithelium is shaped and layered to suit protection, absorption or secretion.
questions.explanation: Simple (4), compound and glandular with locations and functions.

questions.question: Give an account of connective tissue, describing the loose, dense and specialised types with examples.
questions.answer: Connective tissue binds, supports and packs other tissues, with its cells scattered in an abundant non-living matrix. LOOSE connective tissue: (a) AREOLAR tissue fills spaces in organs, supports and repairs, and joins skin to muscle, containing fibroblasts, mast cells and macrophages; (b) ADIPOSE tissue stores fat below the skin and around organs, insulating and cushioning the body. DENSE connective tissue has closely packed fibres forming strong cords: TENDONS join muscle to bone and LIGAMENTS join bone to bone. SPECIALISED (supportive and fluid) connective tissues: CARTILAGE has a firm flexible matrix with chondrocytes and supports the nose, ear pinna and joints; BONE has a hard matrix hardened by calcium and phosphate salts with osteocytes around Haversian canals and forms the skeleton; and BLOOD is a fluid connective tissue with a plasma matrix carrying red cells (oxygen), white cells (defence) and platelets (clotting). Together these tissues connect and support the whole body.
questions.explanation: Loose, dense and specialised connective tissues with examples.

questions.question: Describe blood as a connective tissue, explaining its composition and the functions of each component.
questions.answer: Blood is a FLUID connective tissue because it has cells suspended in an abundant liquid matrix and it connects and transports materials between body parts. Its liquid matrix, PLASMA (about 55% of blood), is water containing proteins, salts, glucose, hormones and wastes; plasma transports these dissolved substances and helps distribute heat. Suspended in the plasma are the formed elements. RED BLOOD CELLS (erythrocytes) contain the pigment haemoglobin and carry oxygen (and some carbon dioxide). WHITE BLOOD CELLS (leucocytes) defend the body by destroying germs and producing immunity. PLATELETS (thrombocytes) are cell fragments that gather at wounds and help the blood to clot, stopping bleeding. So blood transports gases, nutrients, wastes and hormones, defends against disease and helps in clotting and temperature regulation - all the roles expected of a versatile connective tissue.
questions.explanation: Plasma + RBC/WBC/platelets with functions; why it is connective.

questions.question: Describe the three types of muscular tissue and the structure of nervous tissue, and explain how each contributes to the working of the body.
questions.answer: MUSCULAR TISSUE produces movement through contractile fibres. SKELETAL (striated, voluntary) muscle has long, cylindrical, unbranched, multinucleate fibres with striations; attached to bones, it moves the skeleton under conscious control. SMOOTH (unstriated, involuntary) muscle has spindle-shaped single-nucleate cells without striations; found in the walls of the stomach, intestine and blood vessels, it moves food and other materials slowly and automatically. CARDIAC muscle has cylindrical, branched fibres joined at intercalated discs; striated but involuntary, it forms the heart wall and contracts rhythmically throughout life to pump blood. NERVOUS TISSUE conducts impulses for control and coordination. Its unit, the NEURON, has a cell body (with the nucleus), dendrites that receive impulses and carry them toward the cell body, and a single long axon that carries the impulse away to the next cell across a synapse. Supporting NEUROGLIA hold and nourish the neurons. Together, muscle tissue moves the body and its organs, while nervous tissue senses stimuli and rapidly coordinates the responses.
questions.explanation: Three muscle types + neuron structure + their body roles.

questions.question: Explain how the three tissue systems of a plant and the idea of an organ show division of labour, using the leaf as an example.
questions.answer: A plant's tissues are grouped into three TISSUE SYSTEMS, each with its own job. The EPIDERMAL (dermal) system is the outer epidermis with a waterproof cuticle and stomata; it protects the plant and controls gas exchange and water loss. The GROUND (fundamental) system - cortex, pith and mesophyll, made largely of parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma - carries out photosynthesis, storage and support. The VASCULAR (conducting) system - xylem and phloem in the vascular bundles (veins) - transports water, minerals and food. A LEAF is an ORGAN because it is built from all three systems working together: the epidermis (with stomata) covers and protects it and lets gases in, the mesophyll (ground tissue) full of chloroplasts makes food by photosynthesis, and the vascular bundles (veins) bring water to the mesophyll and carry away the food it makes. Each tissue does a different task, and their cooperation lets the leaf function efficiently - a clear example of DIVISION OF LABOUR, in which specialisation of parts makes the whole organ (and plant) work better than any single tissue could alone.
questions.explanation: Three tissue systems + leaf as organ + division of labour.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a growing sunflower plant, cells at the very tip of the shoot are small, thin-walled and dividing rapidly, while cells lower down have enlarged and specialised. A ring of dividing cells in the older stem is making the stem thicker each year.
(a) Name the meristem at the shoot tip and the growth it causes.
(b) Name the ring of dividing cells in the older stem and the growth it causes.
(c) State two features of the dividing cells at the tip.
(d) To which broad category (meristematic or permanent) do the enlarged specialised cells belong?
questions.answer: (a) The shoot-tip meristem is the APICAL meristem; it causes primary growth, increasing the LENGTH of the plant. (b) The ring of dividing cells is the LATERAL meristem (vascular cambium); it causes secondary growth, increasing the GIRTH/thickness of the stem. (c) The dividing cells are small and thin-walled with dense cytoplasm, large nuclei and little or no vacuole (any two). (d) The enlarged, specialised cells belong to PERMANENT tissue.
questions.explanation: Apical/primary, cambium/secondary, meristem features, permanent tissue.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A florist notices that the young stalk of a leaf can bend in the wind without breaking, whereas the husk of a coconut and the shell of a walnut are extremely hard. When she cuts a pear she feels a gritty texture.
(a) Which living tissue gives the leaf stalk its flexible support?
(b) Where in that tissue is the wall thickening deposited?
(c) Which dead tissue gives hardness to the walnut shell?
(d) Name the cells that cause the gritty texture of the pear.
questions.answer: (a) COLLENCHYMA gives flexible mechanical support to the young leaf stalk. (b) Its wall thickening is deposited at the CORNERS of the cells (cellulose and pectin). (c) SCLERENCHYMA gives the walnut shell its hardness, its cells having thick lignified walls. (d) The gritty texture of the pear is caused by SCLEREIDS (stone cells).
questions.explanation: Collenchyma/corners; sclerenchyma; sclereids.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
When a tree trunk is 'ringed' - a complete strip of bark and the tissue just inside it removed all round - the leaves above stay green for a while but the roots below slowly starve, and swelling appears just above the cut. The wood inside continues to carry water up to the leaves.
(a) Which tissue was removed with the bark, causing the roots to starve?
(b) What is the movement of food in that tissue called?
(c) Which tissue in the wood still carries water up?
(d) Why do the roots starve while the leaves stay green?
questions.answer: (a) The PHLOEM (in the bark) was removed, cutting off food supply to the roots. (b) The movement of food in phloem is called TRANSLOCATION. (c) The XYLEM in the wood still carries water and minerals upward. (d) The roots starve because phloem, which carries food downward from the leaves, has been cut; the leaves stay green because xylem is intact and still supplies water, and the leaves keep making food that now accumulates above the cut (the swelling).
questions.explanation: Phloem/translocation; xylem carries water; roots cut off from food.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A cross-section of a young stem shows an outer single layer of cells covered by a waxy film, an inner region of soft packing tissue with some green cells, and bundles containing water- and food-conducting tissue.
(a) Name the outer single layer and the waxy film on it.
(b) To which tissue system does the soft packing tissue belong?
(c) Name the two conducting tissues in the bundles.
(d) To which tissue system do those bundles belong?
questions.answer: (a) The outer single layer is the EPIDERMIS, covered by a waxy CUTICLE. (b) The soft packing tissue (with green cells) belongs to the GROUND (fundamental) tissue system. (c) The two conducting tissues are XYLEM and PHLOEM. (d) The bundles belong to the VASCULAR (conducting) tissue system.
questions.explanation: Epidermis/cuticle; ground system; xylem and phloem; vascular system.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The wall of the small intestine is lined by tall, closely packed cells that absorb digested food; scattered among them are cells that pour out mucus. The air sacs of the lungs, by contrast, are lined by extremely thin flat cells across which oxygen diffuses into the blood.
(a) Name the tall lining epithelium of the intestine.
(b) Name the flat epithelium of the air sacs.
(c) Why is the flat epithelium suited to the air sacs?
(d) What is the type of epithelium formed by the mucus-secreting cells called?
questions.answer: (a) The tall lining epithelium of the intestine is COLUMNAR epithelium. (b) The flat epithelium of the air sacs is SQUAMOUS epithelium. (c) Squamous cells are extremely thin and flat, so gases such as oxygen can diffuse across them quickly and easily. (d) The mucus-secreting cells form GLANDULAR epithelium (goblet cells).
questions.explanation: Columnar; squamous; thin for diffusion; glandular.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
An athlete tears the cord that attaches her calf muscle to her heel bone, and also sprains the cord that holds two bones together at her ankle. Her doctor explains that both are made of dense connective tissue but connect different structures.
(a) Name the cord joining muscle to bone.
(b) Name the cord joining bone to bone.
(c) To which broad category of tissue do both belong?
(d) State the general feature that makes a tissue 'connective'.
questions.answer: (a) The cord joining muscle to bone is a TENDON. (b) The cord joining bone to bone is a LIGAMENT. (c) Both belong to CONNECTIVE tissue (dense connective tissue). (d) A connective tissue has its cells scattered in an abundant non-living matrix and serves to bind, support and connect other tissues and organs.
questions.explanation: Tendon; ligament; connective tissue; cells in matrix that bind/support.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A blood report shows a very low red-cell count and low haemoglobin (anaemia), a raised white-cell count during an infection, and a low platelet count. The plasma is normal.
(a) Which gas transport suffers when red cells and haemoglobin are low?
(b) Why does the white-cell count rise during infection?
(c) What problem is expected from the low platelet count?
(d) Name the fluid matrix that remains normal.
questions.answer: (a) OXYGEN transport suffers, because red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; the person feels tired and breathless. (b) White blood cells defend the body against disease, so their number rises during infection to fight the germs. (c) A low platelet count means poor CLOTTING, so cuts bleed for a long time and bruising occurs easily. (d) The normal fluid matrix is the PLASMA.
questions.explanation: Oxygen transport; WBC defence; poor clotting; plasma.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
When you decide to lift a cup, muscles attached to your arm bones contract quickly and then tire after a while. Meanwhile, without any decision on your part, the muscle in your gut wall slowly pushes food along, and your heart muscle beats steadily hour after hour without tiring.
(a) Name the muscle type that lifts the cup and say whether it is voluntary or involuntary.
(b) Name the muscle type in the gut wall.
(c) Name the muscle type in the heart and one special structure joining its fibres.
(d) Which of these three does not tire?
questions.answer: (a) The muscle that lifts the cup is SKELETAL (striated) muscle; it is VOLUNTARY (under conscious control). (b) The muscle in the gut wall is SMOOTH (unstriated, involuntary) muscle. (c) The heart is made of CARDIAC muscle, whose branched fibres are joined by INTERCALATED DISCS. (d) CARDIAC muscle does not tire; it beats steadily throughout life.
questions.explanation: Skeletal/voluntary; smooth; cardiac/intercalated discs; cardiac untiring.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
When a person touches a hot object, a message is picked up by fine branched endings of a nerve cell in the skin, travels along the cell to a long fibre, and is passed on to the next nerve cell so the hand is pulled away almost at once. Other cells around the nerve cell merely support and nourish it.
(a) Name the nerve cell and its branched receiving endings.
(b) Name the long fibre that carries the message onward.
(c) What is the junction where the message passes to the next cell called?
(d) Name the supporting cells.
questions.answer: (a) The nerve cell is a NEURON; its branched receiving endings are the DENDRITES. (b) The long fibre carrying the message onward is the AXON. (c) The junction to the next cell is a SYNAPSE. (d) The supporting cells are NEUROGLIA (glial cells).
questions.explanation: Neuron/dendrites; axon; synapse; neuroglia.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A biology class examines four prepared slides: (i) small dividing cells at a root tip, (ii) dead thick-walled fibres from jute, (iii) flat tile-like cells from the lining of a lung air sac, and (iv) cells lying in tiny spaces (lacunae) within a firm but flexible matrix from the ear pinna.
(a) Slide (i) - name the tissue category and the growth it causes.
(b) Slide (ii) - name the tissue.
(c) Slide (iii) - name the epithelium.
(d) Slide (iv) - name the tissue and its cells.
questions.answer: (a) Slide (i) is MERISTEMATIC tissue (apical meristem); it causes primary growth, increasing length. (b) Slide (ii) is SCLERENCHYMA (fibres). (c) Slide (iii) is SQUAMOUS epithelium. (d) Slide (iv) is CARTILAGE, and its cells are CHONDROCYTES.
questions.explanation: Meristematic/length; sclerenchyma; squamous; cartilage/chondrocytes.
